lead: Two ways to share one machine are common today. A virtual machine runs a whole guest operating system on emulated hardware, managed by a hypervisor such as KVM. A container runs a single process tree with its own view of the file system, managed by Docker on the host kernel. The first gives strong isolation and a free choice of operating system; the second starts in under a second and packs small. Administrators use both: containers for services, virtual machines for guests that need their own kernel.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 on processes and signals, and Chapter 4.5 on ports and remote access.

blocks.text: Virtualization runs more than one system on one physical computer. The real machine is the host. Each system it runs is a guest, and the guest believes it owns a complete computer: its own CPU count, memory, disks and network cards.
The software that creates and supervises guests is the hypervisor. It hands out CPU time, memory, disk and network cards to each guest and keeps guests apart. Hypervisors come in two types.

items: Type 1 runs directly on the hardware, with nothing between guest instructions and the CPU. KVM, Xen and VMware ESXi are type 1.
Type 2 runs as an ordinary program on an installed operating system. VirtualBox and VMware Workstation are type 2; you start them like any application.

blocks.text: KVM (Kernel-based Virtual Machine) is a Linux kernel module, so the host kernel itself acts as the hypervisor. It is classed as type 1 because guest code executes directly on the CPU. The module needs hardware virtualization support — Intel VT-x or AMD-V — switched on in the BIOS.

Why bother? One server with 64 GB of RAM can hold ten guests of 4 GB instead of sitting half idle. A broken test guest is deleted and recreated. Two teams each get their own kernel version on one box. The cost is weight: every guest carries its own kernel, boot process and device drivers.

sections.h3: KVM: the guest has its own kernel

blocks.text: Three parts make KVM work. The kvm module in the host kernel provides the device /dev/kvm; check it with lsmod | grep kvm, which usually shows kvm_intel or kvm_amd. QEMU emulates the guest's hardware — disk controller, network card, display — while KVM lets the guest's instructions run on the real CPU. libvirt is a service that stores each guest's XML definition and starts it.
virsh talks to libvirt. virsh list --all shows every defined guest and its state: running, shut off or paused. virsh start webvm boots one. virsh shutdown webvm asks the guest to shut down cleanly.
virt-install creates a new guest in one command:

The flags mean: --name is the guest name, --ram is memory in MB, --vcpus is virtual CPUs, --disk gives a disk image file and its size in GB, --cdrom is the install medium. The guest boots the installer once, installs its own kernel, and from then on boots that kernel itself. Only a few syllabi teach the KVM command set in detail; most want you to know that the guest owns a kernel and that virsh manages it.

A container is a process, or a small tree of processes, started with three restrictions: Linux namespaces give it its own file system, its own process list and its own network; cgroups limit its CPU and memory. It uses the host kernel, not a second one.

An image is a read-only bundle of files plus a starting command. A container is a running instance of an image with a thin writable layer on top, and that layer disappears when the container is removed. A Dockerfile describes the image:

blocks.code:
FROM nginx:alpine
COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/
EXPOSE 80
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

blocks.text: FROM names the base image, COPY adds files, EXPOSE records the port the service listens on, and CMD is the process that becomes PID 1 inside the container. When that process exits, the container stops. A container is not a machine that idles.

items: docker build -t web:v1 . builds an image named web with tag v1. The dot is the build context — the directory sent to the builder, which must contain the Dockerfile.
docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name web web:v1 starts a container. -d detaches it from the terminal, --name names it, -p publishes a port.
docker ps lists running containers with ID, image, command, ports and name; docker ps -a also shows stopped ones.
docker stop web sends SIGTERM, waits, then SIGKILL. docker rm web deletes the stopped container.

blocks.text: Port mapping reads host first, container second: -p 8080:80 forwards host port 8080 to port 80 inside. A bind mount -v /srv/site:/usr/share/nginx/html puts a host directory inside the container, so edits appear at once. A volume -v webdata:/var/lib/mysql is storage Docker manages for you and keeps after the container is gone.
A container shares the host kernel; a virtual machine runs its own. Everything else follows from that one line.

Use a container for a stateless web service, a build agent, or a database with a volume. Use a virtual machine when you need a different kernel or a different operating system, or when the workload is untrusted.

examples.question: An administrator builds a web image from a Dockerfile and runs it, then creates a KVM guest. The host port is 8080, the service port inside the container is 80, the image is web:v1, and the guest webvm gets 2 vCPUs and 2048 MB of RAM with a 10 GB disk. Give every command, the line docker ps prints, and state which of the two uses the host kernel.
steps: Build the image: docker build -t web:v1 . The dot is the context; the Dockerfile in that directory is read and the image gets the name web and tag v1.
Run it detached: docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name web web:v1. Docker prints a container ID, for example a1b2c3. Host port 8080 now forwards to container port 80.

Check the ports: docker ps prints a line with ID a1b2c3, image web:v1, command "nginx -g 'daemon off;'", ports 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp and name web. A browser on the host at http://localhost:8080 reaches nginx on port 80 inside the container.
Stop and remove: docker stop web, then docker rm web. The writable layer is discarded; the image web:v1 stays on disk.

Create the guest: virt-install --name webvm --ram 2048 --vcpus 2 --disk path=/var/lib/libvirt/images/webvm.qcow2,size=10 --cdrom /iso/debian.iso. It gets 2 vCPUs, 2048 MB = 2 GB of RAM, and a 10 GB disk file.
Confirm the guest after installation: virsh list --all shows webvm in the running state.

Who shares the host kernel? The container does. Docker starts a process tree on the host kernel with namespaces and cgroups. The guest webvm runs its own kernel on the virtual CPUs that KVM schedules.
examples.answer: The container shares the host kernel; the guest webvm gets 2 vCPUs and 2048 MB (2 GB) of RAM with a 10 GB disk and boots its own kernel.
examples.check:
host_port = 8080
container_port = 80
vcpus = 2
ram_mb = 2048
print(host_port)
print(container_port)
print(vcpus)
print(ram_mb)
print(ram_mb / 1024)

traps: In -p 8080:80 the host port comes first and the container port second. Writing -p 80:8080 forwards host 80 to container 8080, which is the opposite of what most students mean.
A container is not a lightweight virtual machine. It has no own kernel, no init system by default and no idle state; its main process exiting ends it.
docker stop and docker rm are different: stop ends the process, rm deletes the container and its writable layer. Neither removes the image.
The dot in docker build -t web:v1 . is the build context, not decoration. Leave it out and the build fails with a missing Dockerfile or wrong path.
Without -d, docker run attaches to the terminal and holds it until the process exits. Examiners often show a missing -d as the reason a shell appeared to hang.

quiz.q: Define image and container in one sentence each.
quiz.a: An image is a read-only bundle of files plus a starting command. A container is a running instance of an image with a thin writable layer on top.

quiz.q: What does virsh list --all display, and which service does it query?
quiz.a: Every defined guest and its state (running, shut off, paused). It queries the libvirt service.

quiz.q: Why does a container stop as soon as its main process exits, while a virtual machine keeps running until you shut it down?
quiz.a: The container is only a process tree wrapped in namespaces and cgroups; PID 1 exiting ends the tree, so nothing remains. A virtual machine runs its own kernel, which keeps running as a guest until the guest is shut down or the hypervisor stops it.

quiz.q: Write the commands to build an image tagged api:v2 from the current directory, then run it detached with name api so that host port 8000 reaches port 5000 inside.
quiz.a: docker build -t api:v2 . then docker run -d -p 8000:5000 --name api api:v2.

quiz.q: A container is run with -p 9090:80. Which URL on the host reaches the service, and which port is the service listening on inside the container?
quiz.a: http://localhost:9090 on the host; the service listens on port 80 inside the container.

quiz.q: A team wants to replace twenty virtual machines with containers, but one service is a Windows-only application. What must stay a virtual machine and why?
quiz.a: The Windows service must stay a virtual machine. Containers share the host Linux kernel, so they cannot provide a Windows kernel; a virtual machine runs its own guest kernel and can be Windows. The other nineteen Linux services can move to containers, saving RAM and boot time.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, containers are rarely run by hand: an orchestrator such as Kubernetes or Docker Swarm schedules them across many hosts, and Docker Compose starts a group of containers on one host. Newer designs blur the line — Kata Containers and Firecracker microVMs run each container inside a tiny virtual machine for stronger isolation. Search for runc, containerd, OCI image spec and libvirt XML to go deeper, and try docker inspect on a running container to see the namespaces and cgroups it actually uses.
